The Japanese Zhongyuan Command's rear hospital for the wounded had once been the canteen of Wuchang University—two stories, at the foot of Mount Luojia. To ease the wounded men's homesickness, the ground before the wards had been planted thick with cherry trees. Come spring, the white petals scattered over the paths like flakes of snow.

Each time Jiang Yongnan came out of the wards he thought of his student days in Kyoto, but the daze of it passed in an instant. He would look down and see his regulation army boots treading those petals, as though with every step he trod on his own naked body.
The priest always consoled him with a Chinese proverb: a great man can bend and can stretch—you are a man.

"What you want is to make use of this uniform I wear." Jiang Yongnan had come to the church one night after drinking, and he looked at the priest, drunk. "But be quick about it. I'm afraid I won't hold out—I'll cut their arteries on the operating table."
"You will not." The priest shook his head. "You must believe this is God's testing of us."

"To hell with your God." More and more, Jiang Yongnan felt he had become a coarse Japanese soldier himself, above all on the nights when he spoke their language and drank with the young officers of the command, listening to them sing the ballads of their homeland.

Yet more often than not he would change out of the uniform and, in plain clothes, sit giving free treatment in the church, helping the priest tend the poor who came for care. It was over this that the chief medical officer called him into the office one day and took from a drawer a file sent up by the military police. When Jiang Yongnan had skimmed it, the chief medical officer said, "It's no good thing to catch the eye of the disciplinary branch—least of all for a Korean officer."
"But I am first of all a doctor." Jiang Yongnan closed the folder and stood straight. "You are a doctor too. On our first day in medical school we all swore to keep the oath of Hippocrates."

"You really are a bookish fool . . . War is the very thing made to destroy oaths." The chief medical officer heaved a long sigh, drew a pen from his breast pocket, and scrawled two lines on a prescription slip, which he handed to Jiang Yongnan. "Go and find this Kosaka. Perhaps he can get you past this."

Kosaka Jirō was a reporter posted to the three towns of Wuhan by the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shimbun. A few days after meeting Jiang Yongnan he ran a series of dispatches under the title "A Korean Military Doctor in Shina," interviewing the priest and a great many of the poor Jiang Yongnan had treated, and running photographs from the scene besides. As a model instance of "building the Greater East Asia Sphere together in common prosperity," the reports were soon reprinted in Chinese, Japanese, and Korean papers alike. For this Jiang Yongnan received a commendation by general order of the Japanese high command and was promoted, out of the usual course, to lieutenant.
The night of his commission Jiang Yongnan drank himself blind, and woke to find himself lying on the cold steps of the church, his head splitting.

Without a word the priest helped him into the bedroom, brewed a cup of barley tea, stripped off his uniform, and sat down to one side; then, like a housewife, he took up a rag, wet it, and carefully wiped the filth from that uniform.

"There's no washing me clean now, not if I leapt into the Yellow River." Jiang Yongnan delivered the Chinese proverb in an imitation of the priest's manner, laughed a long, bitter laugh, and then switched to Korean. "This too is what you people want, isn't it?"
The priest smiled, and looked at him with a peculiarly serene expression. "To go on living in the wolves' den, you have to be more wolf than the wolves."
"But I don't want to live in it another day." Jiang Yongnan flung out his hand, and the tea bowl on the table smashed to the floor into countless pieces.

"You chose the road yourself, and you must walk it to the end, one step at a time." The priest said it word by word, and the look he turned on Jiang Yongnan sharpened, pushing into him little by little, until the whole man sagged into the chair like a deflated ball. The plum-rain season that came soon after was sodden and stifling, and the city of Wuchang was like something shut up in a steamer that would never come to a boil.

The dusk on which the priest came for Jiang Yongnan could not decide between clear and rain. Dressed in the hemp-cloth jacket of a servant, an oiled-paper umbrella tucked under his arm, he stood at a corner the hospital gatehouse could not see, and by the time Jiang Yongnan came out with a few of the other medical officers the street lamps had come on.

Jiang Yongnan looked straight through him and passed him, and only long after did he turn back to stand before him. "So the day has come, it seems, that I've been waiting for." The priest said nothing. He turned and led him through the streets and lanes to the door of a restaurant, where he stopped and said, without looking back, "There's still time to turn around now."

Jiang Yongnan said nothing. He only took off his army cap, wiped the sweat from his forehead with a handkerchief, and was the first to set foot on the restaurant steps. The Mr. Qi who rose to meet them in the private room was an intelligence man of the Nationalist government. When he had made his brief introductions the priest did not sit, but gave Jiang Yongnan one long look, turned, and left.

"We too act only because we must." Mr. Qi's face was grave and resigned. As he spoke he passed over a photograph—a Nationalist colonel in full uniform. When he was sure Jiang Yongnan had fixed the face in memory, Mr. Qi took the photograph back and set it aside. "The Tokko will bring this man to your hospital tomorrow . . . for a small operation."
"You want to save him inside the hospital?" said Jiang Yongnan.

Mr. Qi was silent a moment. "To save a man at the very heart of the Zhongyuan Command is harder than climbing to heaven." As he spoke he took out a silver dollar, laid it on the table, and pushed it gently toward Jiang Yongnan. "You must find a way to get it into his hand."
"As simple as that?" Jiang Yongnan asked.
Mr. Qi nodded. He picked up his wine cup, took a small sip, set it down, then took up his chopsticks, lifted a piece of stir-fried kidney, and chewed it in silence.
Jiang Yongnan picked up the silver dollar and soon found it was only a finely made box; pinching both sides, he pulled it hard apart, and saw inside a thin, sealed layer of wax.
"What is this?"
Mr. Qi raised his eyes and said it without evasion: "Potassium cyanide."

Guo Bingyan's operation was only the removal of an acutely inflamed appendix, yet the Japanese rear hospital braced as though for a great enemy. Not only were extra military police brought in to seal off the second-floor ward, but iron bars were fitted to the windows of the special-care room to keep the prisoner from leaping out. Tokko field men kept watch in the corridor twenty-four hours a day, questioning every doctor and nurse who entered; even the cleaning of the patient's wound and the changing of his dressings went on under the close guard of an agent and an interpreter.

On the third day after the operation Jiang Yongnan came at dusk to make his rounds. Beyond the necessary examination he said almost nothing, only stood at the bedside turning the ward record page by page until the nurse had changed the gauze and pulled the patient's trousers back up. Jiang Yongnan snapped shut the lead cover of the ward record and handed it across the bed to the nurse. Only then did Guo Bingyan notice the watch on the medical officer's wrist: the hands had stopped at twenty past two.

Coming out of the ward Jiang Yongnan seemed to remember something, and said to the interpreter in Japanese, "Go and tell the patient not to fear the pain. After surgery he should get up and move about, go and sit in the sofa a while; it wards off adhesions of the bowel."
The interpreter said respectfully, "Yes, sir."

In the dead of night Guo Bingyan slipped from the bed and found, between the arm and the cushion of the sofa, a gauze bundle wrapped around a screwdriver, a scalpel, a syringe, and an ampoule of morphine. First he backed the screws off two of the iron bars with the screwdriver, then lay quietly down again; and when the distant clock tower had struck twice, he began to count off the seconds in his mind, injected the morphine into his body, and with the scalpel cut the bedsheet into strips and knotted them together.

Guo Bingyan climbed down from the window on the sheets, his wound long since split open. He felt the warm blood soak through the gauze and stain his trousers. Jiang Yongnan gave him only a glance, steadied him around to the back, and helped him climb through an open window into the duty doctors' rest room.
"Whose orders do you take?" Guo Bingyan did not speak until Jiang Yongnan had finished binding the wound, had him change into a medical officer's uniform, and pulled a white coat on over it.
"Come with me to the ward." As he spoke Jiang Yongnan handed him a surgical mask.

The first to find the prisoner gone from the window was the nurse bringing medicine; she had only opened her mouth when the agent with her let out a shout, and the military police blew their whistles. The rear hospital fell at once into chaos, boots pounding everywhere down the ward corridors. Pursuit and search began almost together. Armed military police burst into every ward, checked the patient in each bed, and ordered the doctors and nurses to wait where they stood, no one permitted to leave the ward. Before long they found a ladder laid against the hospital's outer wall. Jiang Yongnan stood in the ward until the sound of the military police's boots had left the building, then gave Guo Bingyan a look. But just as they were crossing the corridor, a military policeman appeared out of nowhere.
Drawing his pistol, he said, "Halt."

Guo Bingyan waited until the military policeman had come close; the instant he pulled off his mask, his other hand flew up, and the scalpel opened the man's windpipe and carotid together. The blood sprayed out, and the military policeman clutched his neck and made a gurgling sound on the floor. Pressing his own belly, which had begun to seep blood again, Guo Bingyan picked up the pistol and said to the young medical officer, who still stood there stunned, "Don't just stand there."

Toward dawn Guo Bingyan was near shock from loss of blood. In a small boat at the edge of East Lake Jiang Yongnan stitched the wound closed again, and after they had waited out the whole day, it took him a whole night to row the boat to the far shore.

The little boat had been hired a full two days and had lain all that while in the reeds at the edge of East Lake, loaded with food, clothing, and his medical case. Jiang Yongnan had spent two days going carefully over every route the escape would have to take. Before that he had done one thing more: before Guo Bingyan was ever brought to the hospital, he had tucked the gauze bundle between the arm and the cushion of the sofa in the special-care room.

Two days on, Guo Bingyan's fever broke. In a derelict thatched hut in a deserted village he watched Jiang Yongnan without a flicker, watched until the young man lowered his head. And when Jiang Yongnan raised it again, what he met was the black bore of a gun.

"I'm not one of your people. I only changed your plan." Jiang Yongnan, having recounted that meeting with Mr. Qi, drew out the silver dollar and set it on the straw mat. "I imagine you know better than I do what is inside it."
Guo Bingyan looked calmly at the young man before him. "Do you know the consequence of changing a plan on your own authority?"

"For me it comes to the same thing either way." Jiang Yongnan paused a little, then spoke frankly. If the rescue had failed, he said, he would surely have been taken for a Chinese agent and died a wretched death in the Tokko's torture rooms. And if it succeeded, he might well not live either: he would fall under the same suspicion, taken for a Japanese spy trying to burrow into the Nationalist intelligence service, and executed—exactly as he was about to be now. His eyes fell again to the silver dollar, then came quickly back to Guo Bingyan. "And did you think that if you'd swallowed the poison, the Japanese wouldn't have hunted down where it came from?" Jiang Yongnan shook his head. "They'd have traced it to me soon enough. Either way, I don't live."
Guo Bingyan said nothing. He still held the pistol level, and the look he turned on Jiang Yongnan was as overcast as the sky outside.

Jiang Yongnan's mouth broke open and, of all things, he smiled like a child. He smiled and said, "Aren't you about to tell me, too, that I could just throw the thing away, pretend none of it ever happened, and go on being your Japanese army doctor? That I could even hand it over to the Tokko?" As he spoke Jiang Yongnan slowly drew the smile back off his face. He bore down on the gaunt, haggard middle-aged man before him with a gaze that was almost cruel, and meeting those overcast eyes he went on, "And if I did . . . tell me, would your people let me live?"
